titleEn: [Smart Power Meter EnerTalk] How much electricity does our air conditioner use? EnerTalk when you're curious
contentEn:
These days, there's a lot of buzz about AI and VR/AR, but a year or two ago, IoT and big data were all the rage. It's true that despite these technologies, there weren't many standout products. Was it all just hype? I don't think so. When things get noisy, it means investors are flocking, and planning and development take time. It can take as little as 6 months, and if hardware is involved, that period can be even longer. Among these, I'd like to introduce you to EnerTalk, a domestic smart power meter. This post was written after being selected as an EnerTalk experience group member. I originally planned to write it sooner, but I wanted to check the electricity bill after a full month of usage following installation, so it took a little longer.

1. What is the Smart Power Meter EnerTalk?

It's a smart device that connects to your home's wireless LAN to provide real-time electricity usage, predict electricity bills based on usage, and allow comparison with other households.

{{IMG:1}}
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        **EnerTalk (Our Home's Electricity Usage Guide) Electricity bill measurement, power consumption measurement, standby power, progressive rate management, electricity bill shock management, electricity bill saving, patented product, energy saving meter, electricity saving, electricity bill reduction device**
                                        
                Seller
                
            
                EnerTalk
                *npay_available*
            
        
                Price
                
            
                65,000 won
            
        
            
                                    
                                
                            

http://storefarm.naver.com/enertalk/products/414863942

EnerTalk is the same product as LG Uplus's IoT Energy Meter.

{{IMG:2}}

However, if you install it through LG Uplus, it's difficult to get proper service unless you subscribe to LG Uplus's wired internet network. In short, you're tied to the Uplus communication network. I initially considered this product but ultimately gave up because I didn't want to change my home's IPTV from KT.

2. Installation

First, the installation. I had it installed on May 20, 2016. A technician visited. Of course, the technician visit is separate from the device cost. However, if you're not afraid of handling electricity, installation is not too difficult. Since I was part of the experience group, I received a visit to hear the explanation.

1) Open the distribution board (fuse box).

First, the distribution board. My apartment is an e-Pyeonhan Sesang apartment built in June 2007, so I assume similar brands would be similar.

{{IMG:3}}
                                
                            Apartment Distribution Board

When you open it, it looks like this. I'll connect it to the circuit breaker on the far right.

{{IMG:4}}

2) Product check

The components are simple: an electric wire, the EnerTalk main unit. That wire will supply electricity from the circuit breaker to the EnerTalk main unit. The loop-like part on top of EnerTalk is actually the power consumption meter. I'll open the loop and clamp it onto the main power line.

{{IMG:5}}

3) Power supply

Loosen the screws on the distribution board and EnerTalk, connect them with the enclosed wire, tighten them, and then turn on the power. A light will come on like this. This means EnerTalk is receiving power normally. When connecting, always turn off the switch of the circuit breaker you are connecting to.

{{IMG:6}}

4) Sensor installation

The sensor opens like this.

{{IMG:7}}
                                
                            EnerTalk Power Measurement Sensor

I guess it measures the strength of the magnetic field when electricity flows. Clamp it firmly onto the main electrical wire's insulation. Then, organize the equipment. My home's distribution board didn't have much extra space, but it fit somehow. Then, close it. For more detailed photos regarding EnerTalk installation, you can refer to other blogs.

{{IMG:8}}

3. App Connection

Naturally, you need a Wi-Fi router at home; 2.4Ghz connection is supported. Install the EnerTalk app.

[**EnerTalk HOME - 에너톡 - Android app on Google Play** play.google.com](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.ionicframework.enertalkhome874425)

After signing up, it connects with EnerTalk for the first time and searches for your router. You select your home's router, enter the password, and this tells EnerTalk about your home's router, establishing the connection. I considered taking screenshots of each step, but I don't think it's necessary, so I'll just explain this much.

4. Let's see how much electricity our house uses in a month.

For detailed settings, you can call your apartment management office to find out when electricity bills are tallied. My apartment said it was the 10th of every month. However, when I checked this month's bill, it was different.

{{IMG:9}}

{{IMG:10}}

I called the management office, and it turns out the June bill covers May 10th to June 9th.

{{IMG:11}}

9 days of usage weren't measured. ㅜㅜ It seems I'll have to wait another month for accurate figures. Since my moving date was included, there will likely be a significant error. This way, you can directly see how many Kwh you used each month. Seeing it with my own eyes, the difference between August and June is huge!

5. Realizing the power of electricity-guzzling air conditioners.

I recently received an unfamiliar alarm.

{{IMG:12}}

Huh... what's this? I didn't have this last month. So I checked... Wow. It's going up like this because I've been running the air conditioner due to the heat. The difference between the 19th and the 24th is enormous.

{{IMG:13}}

Comparing the two days by hour, on the 19th, I only ran the air conditioner briefly around 6 PM. On Sunday, July 24th, I spent the whole day at home with the kids, so I kept the air conditioner on continuously. Even playing at home isn't free. It seems I spent about 1500 won on the air conditioner that day.

{{IMG:14}}

6. Does our house use a lot?

It's hard to confirm with absolute figures since it's grouped by apartment size and the range of family members is wide, but fortunately, we don't use much. ^^

{{IMG:15}}

7. Other features

EnerTalk provides an Open API, allowing you to create your own services. A hackathon related to this was held recently. And I know they are planning to offer an "energy fingerprint" feature. If enough of this data accumulates, we can understand the characteristics of how different appliances consume electricity, which could lead to more efficient electricity usage habits. I expect we might even be able to tell if the air conditioner is on or if it's a hairdryer based on electricity usage patterns, especially if we utilize big data and AI technologies as mentioned earlier. Google acquired the IoT company Nest for 3.2 trillion won. Even in Korea, despite the smaller market, good companies like this are actively working, and the world seems to be gradually becoming smarter. I used to think that by the 21st century, all homes would be smart, but arriving in the actual 21st century, it's fun to gradually change to smart devices one by one.

8. Reasonable electricity bill is needed.

Recently, attorney Kwak Sang-eon, who is also the son-in-law of former President Roh Moo-hyun, has been leading a movement and lawsuit against KEPCO's progressive electricity rate system.

http://news.naver.com/main/read.nhn?mode=LSD&mid=sec&oid=052&aid=0000880333&sid1=001
                                **[Live Economy] Unlawful progressive electricity rates, only households bear the burden** [Live Interview] ■ Broadcast: YTN Radio FM 94.5 (15:10~16:00) ■ Host: Kim Woo-sung PD ■ Interviewee: Kwak Sang-eon, Attorney at Law Firm Ingang ◇ Kim Woo-sung PD (hereinafter Kim Woo-sung)> For several days... news.naver.com

http://news.naver.com/main/read.nhn?mode=LSD&mid=sec&oid=052&aid=0000880333&sid1=001

I agree with this stance. The progressive rate for household electricity seems to have been a policy aimed at supporting Korea's export-oriented economy. It was likely an expression of will to prioritize exports even at the expense of domestic demand. However, with unstable international affairs and diminishing trickle-down effects these days, the argument that domestic demand and consumption significantly impact the national economy and happiness is gaining traction. And I believe this progressive rate is one of the factors hindering domestic demand and consumption. Furthermore, with the advent of electric vehicles, our energy policy needs a paradigm shift. It's time for a reasonable electricity pricing system with price elasticity, where you pay for what you use. Looking at the progressive rate graph makes it even more evident. Wow. To achieve that, it's time for us to look into how much we're actually using. And I believe IoT devices like this are one way to do that.

1. The post I previously wrote as a 'Megal Support Declaration' was actually about the desires within me.

Regarding the meaning of the post where I previously declared support for Megal, I actually don't know Megal well. I wasn't a member there, nor do I agree with the 'trashy' posts they talk about. (I've already written about this in the relevant content.) However, there's another reason why I wrote such a provocative title at the time. **It is a confession that Megal and Ilbe exist within me.** This is to talk about the instincts and desires that everyone possesses, and I say this with the hope that netizens' anger will be discussed in a more constructive direction.

First, let's talk about R-rated content. I don't know much about women, but for men, there are porn videos they've probably seen at least once... These contents often contain misogynistic elements. Conversely, though I don't particularly like it, BL (Boys' Love) content, which women enjoy, often contains misandristic elements. This is essentially about having some sexual objectification and violent fantasies towards the other. While it's possible to express this well literarily, I agree that such adult content is not good for teenagers. So, what I want to say is that desires, like Ilbe and Megal, are inherent in everyone. And I believe there needs to be a space to resolve or at least properly enjoy them. Provided, of course, with adult verification. I think this is necessary for both women and men.

2. But Spaces Where Desires Are Expressed in a Distorted Way

However, **the problem is that spaces like Megal and Ilbe are where desires are expressed and consumed in a distorted way.** Furthermore, a more serious problem is that children can join and view them. Expressing one's desires is actually never a pleasant thing. It's easy to despise each other, and often the target is not a real person but content. It is a clear error to think that enjoying porn will turn someone into a rapist. Just as enjoying BL content doesn't lead to kidnapping middle school students. (Oh, of course, I'm not suggesting it should be allowed for teenagers. This is about adults for now.)

In fact, I believe Lezhin Comics has grown into a content consumption site that plays such a role to some extent. The same goes for subcultures like light novels that are consumed recently.

But... what's surprising is that such content has been expressed unfiltered through communities, fueling each other's emotions, and it even feels like we've reached a point where people can't distinguish between content and reality. If that applies to the administrators, it's even more serious.

Here, I want to talk about DC (DC Inside), not Megal. As I mentioned, my online life started with PC communication, and a certain bulletin board from PC communication became DC, and I heard that it later moved towards sites like Utdae and Ilbe. Considering that era, several assumptions can be made. In the early days, it was a platform teeming with adult men. Surprisingly, it was mainly composed of highly educated individuals. Therefore, they maintained a certain line regarding subculture or their lewd jokes. However, recently, women have emerged as a significant force on the internet, and even children and seniors have joined in, making it no longer a network enjoyed only by university students but by the entire nation.

Therefore, this means that these communities are more likely to cross that line. Moreover, it seems that communities have begun to openly display social conflicts, which is their inherent nature. Once again, I am not talking about Megal or Ilbe.

3. Will Burying Megal Be Okay? I Think Megal Might Just Be the Beginning

More importantly, how can we control the monsters lurking within us or on the internet, Megal and Ilbe?

In this situation, let me ask again. **Will burying Megal end it? Will destroying Lezhin Comics end it? I don't think so. Rather, I see this situation as an opportunity. Is Megal not okay, but DC galleries or Ilbe are? No. Is there any guarantee that Utdae won't be corrupted?**

Who monitors large communities, and who regulates them? The National Intelligence Service? Or who regulates the level of your comments? Should we bring in Chinese personnel for pre-screening? It's not such a simple issue, but a very important one.

I think it's better that Megal has become a social issue without much trouble now. If left as is, someday people might discuss bombing the Blue House on DC, or plot gang rape and human trafficking incidents on Ilbe.

There's no law saying that Korea won't become like Europe. If firearms were allowed in Korea, I actually think it would have already happened. The important thing is that current community structures deepen conflicts, strengthen confirmation bias, and make people think there's nothing to fear when acting as a group. It even makes me think of Japan's Kamikaze.

Therefore, a higher level of discussion is needed now. To prevent the birth of second and third Megals, mirroring, and various 'bugs.' I want to talk about that situation now.

As I mentioned, I don't know much about Megal. It's hard to know the background of a community with such a long history unless you've been actively involved for a long time. In fact, I'm not very interested. **The important thing is that Megalian created the currently enraged people, but in reality, all of this seems to be a phenomenon created by the Korean internet. Was DC the culprit from the start? To say so, there are too many new people who have entered the network.**

I feel that the confirmation bias created by social networks and communities, the diversification of user demographics, and the deepening of social conflicts in Korean society are appearing more easily online. I do want to bring up the topic of regulation, but I'd rather put it aside for now, as my thoughts are still shallow at this point. It seems more thought is needed.

**Attachment. I hadn't written this because it seemed like a shallow and clumsy alternative, but since some people were curious about my thoughts, I'm adding what was on my mind. (If I've thrown a stone, I should offer an alternative. However, if I put too much effort into this, I'll neglect my main work...)**

I believe that communities, like webtoons or app stores, also need a framework of self-regulation. As platforms, they should have operating principles revised based on standard operating principles set by the government, and they must fulfill their duty in regulatory activities. In this process, they might be positioned as adult-only communities, in which case adult verification must be mandatory.

If, from an external perspective, a platform is deemed to have failed in its duties under self-regulation, a complaint can be filed with a central regulatory body, and this will then be resolved through consultation between the regulatory body and the platform.

Of course, given the nature of communities, it's not right to prevent small communities from forming and disappearing. Therefore, I believe that regulation should be mandatory for communities with a certain number of members or more, considering their social influence. And this includes not only Megal, Ilbe, Utdae, Ruliweb, and Miznet, but also Naver and Daum cafes.

(Especially in the case of cafes, they have the nature of local communities, so their impact on offline life is considerable.)

Oh... and I'm not a writer. Why do people keep calling me a writer...?

In my writing, I have never criticized anyone, whether they supported Megal or not. I have never criticized specific individuals or groups in my writing. Criticism from supporters and opponents is different. While I may have responded in a similar tone when feeling upset by sarcastic or unconditionally critical comments, the original text was humble. However, the comments ultimately throw stones at individual 'Megal supporters'.

I was so dumbfounded that I almost spoke more harshly, but fearing the discussion would escalate, I revised the main text to be more polite.

You cannot achieve justice by abandoning reason and self-control. No matter how well it's disguised, it's simply violence.

The current flow of events no longer prioritizes the issue or the truth. Megal has already become a corpse, and violent comments accumulating to criticize Megal are increasing more than the trashy posts left by the Megal camp. Since the internet is search-based, only pages are visible. It's virtually impossible to grasp the full context and authenticity without considerable effort. In other words, the public will ultimately be more exposed to the violent comments from the anti-Megal camp and will inevitably focus on that violence rather than understanding the angry anti-Megal camp. It's natural for progressive figures to increasingly declare their support for Megal.

I hope the anti-Megal camp stops justifying violence. Currently, the actions of the anti-Megal camp even look like mirroring. Megal's mirroring. Megal copied Ilbe, and the anti-Megal camp copied Megal... Acting that way and claiming to be different from Ilbe is useless.

1. 정직한 기술 소프트웨어

소프트웨어 강자인 애플의 스마트폰이 삼성전자를 위협하고, 구글의 알파고가 이세돌을 이긴 요즘 소프트웨어는 곡괭이만 데면 부자로 만들어 줄수 있다고 믿는 금광을 보는 듯 한 시선이 느껴진다. 하지만, 소프트웨어는 그 자체로 금광이 될 수는 없다. 소프트웨어의 금언 중에 하나로 여겨지는 GIGO라는 말이 있다. Gold in Gold out. Garbage in Garbage out. 소프트웨어에 대한 기대가 어느때 보다 높아진 지금도 이 가치는 변하지 않았다고 생각한다. 소프트웨어는 많은 혁신을 이루고 있는 것도 분명한 사실이지만, 혁신을 이루는 소프트웨어가 하늘에서 떨어진 것은 아니다. 소프트웨어를 만드는 데는 당연히 사람과 시간과 돈이 필요하며, 혁신을 위한 그만큼의 권한을 가졌을 때에 이루어지는 것이다. 어떠한 영역이 던간에 인정 받지 못하는 소프트웨어는 언제나 주변부를 맴돌 뿐, 혁신의 요소로 동작하기에는 어려움이 있다. 인공지능이 등장한 현 시점에 소프트웨어중심사회라는 단어가 이제는 식상한 듯도 들리지만, 인공지능을 비록한 어떠한 기술이던 간에 해당 영역의 핵심의 자리를 차지하지 않고서는 혁신을 기대하기는 어렵다. 소프트웨어에 그만한 권한과 가치를 메기지 않는 한 어떠한 좋은 기술이던 간에 변화를 만들어내지 못할 것이다. 왜냐하면 소프트웨어를 만드는 개발자는 사람이고, 그 사람들은 나름대로의 인정을 받을 때 움직일 수 있기 때문이다.​

소프트웨어의 위치 변화

과거 소프트웨어 산업은 IT서비스 산업과 패키지소프트웨어를 지칭하는 말이 었다. 그 중 IT서비스가 매우 큰 비중을 차지하였는데 이러한 소프트웨어는 특정 영역의 전산화와 효율을 돕는 지원을 위한 역할을 맡고 있었다. 그러나, 최근 소프트웨어는 이러한 지원의 업무가 아닌 문제를 푸는 주도적 역할을 수행하기 시작했으며, 이에 따라 소프트웨어의 성격이 달라지게 되었다. 이러한 소프트웨어의 특징은 요구사항과 수요자가 명확하지 않으며, 소프트웨어가 문제해결을 위한 적극적인 도구로 사용된다. 이러한 소프트웨어의 성격은 아웃소싱으로 이관이 어려우며 조직내의 자산으로서 소프트웨어의 노하우가 남게 된다. 소프트웨어 기업일수록 물리적 자산보다 훨씬 큰 가치를 갖게 되는데, 소프트웨어가 이렇게 변모할 수 있는 가장 큰 이유는 어떤 특별한 기술의 등장보다는 소프트웨어의 위치와 역할이 더 중요한 요인으로 작용했다.소프트웨어는 기존의 IT서비스 산업에서처럼 프로세스를 최적화하거나 비용을 아끼는데 탁월한 효과가 있는 것도 분명한 사실이지만, 최근 소프트웨어에 거는 기대는 비용감소를 넘어 인공지능을 비롯한 직접 문제해결을 해나가는 소프트웨어를 원한다. 그러나, 이를 위해서는 이러한 소프트웨어는 문제에 접근하고 시도해볼 수 있는 권한을 필요로 하며, 잦은 실패와 실패에 기반한 업무를 수정할 수 있는 권한을 필요로 한다는 사실이 중요하다.기존의 IT서비스의 소프트웨어라면 문제의 발생은 곧 금전적 손실과 배상을 의미했다. 때문에 이를 수업료로 산정할 수는 없었으며, 아무리 좋은 아이디어도 발주자가 또다른 주머니를 열지 않는 한 적용할 수가 없었다. 이 때의 소프트웨어의 최고의 조건은 적은 비용에 틀리지 않게 나오는 것이었다. 이렇게 시작한 전통적인 소프트웨어공학은 요구사항을 어떻게 하면 최대한 달성할 수 있는가를 중심으로 발전되어왔다.

{{IMG:2}}
이미지 출처 : 2014 정보처리 기술지도사 대비 목차잡기 http://goo.gl/b7V91p

그러나, 혁신은 이러한 요구사항이 발견되기 어려운 영역에서 기존의 룰이 적용되지 않는 자기 주도적인 스타트업들로부터 발생했다. 이는 때로는 파괴적이기까지 했는데 앞서 말한 소프트웨어 공학의 기본원리가 최신 방법론안에 전혀 존재하지 않는 것은 아니지만, 프로젝트의 성격이 실패를 가정하고 만들어나간다는 사실은 일을 진행하거나 성과를 측정하는데 매우 다른 양상을 보여주며, 의사결정시에도 큰 영향을 미친다.

{{IMG:3}}
소프트웨어의 최신 방법론

그리고, 이러한 문화는 큰 틀에서 회사의 문화와, 소프트웨어의 개발방법, 아주 작게는 이를 구현하는 코드에도 영향을 준다. 때문에 큰기업이 스타트업의 장점을 받아들인 다는 것은 단순히 개발방법론을 받아들이는 것이 아니라, 개발방법론이 나오게 된 사상과 문화를 받아들이는 일이다. 더군다나 가장 어려운 일은 의사결정자를 포함한 구성원들의 사상개조가 필요하며, 사이클을 돌려보면서 개선되는 것을 체험하는 것이 가장 중요하다. 그러나 오늘날 스타트업을 배우고 체질을 개선하겠다는 기업들이 많은데, 대부분 이러한 구조적 변경을 받아들일 준비가 되었는지 의문이다. 처음에 싸이클이 돌리고, 고객이 항의할 때, 당장 실수하는 것을 지켜볼 수 있는 관리자가 얼마나 될까? 그러나, 우리가 어려운 문제를 풀기를 원한다면 틀리는 것에 대해 인색하지 않아야 하며 결과가 아닌 과정과 체계를 더 중요하게 여겨야 한다. 그것이 소프트웨어적 문화라고 할 수 있다. 이를 위해서는 관리자가 더 스마트해져야 하며 더 디테일 해야 한다. 당연한 이야기겠지만, 스마트하고, 디테일하게 아랫사람을 괴롭히라는 의미가 아니다. 조직원의 개인의 오류를 찾아내는데 힘쓰는 것보다 시스템과 체계에 대해 끊임없이 고민해야 된다는 의미이다. 그리고, 이를 통해 개인을 자연스럽게 변화시키고 개인 스스로가 통제할 수 있게 만드는 것이 중요하다. 강요에 의한 통제는 처음부터 이 방향과 맞지 않다. 소프트웨어가 경험하지 않고서는 그 가치를 느끼기 어려운 것 처럼 이러한 기업문화와 방법은 해보지 않고서는 사실 느끼기 어려운 부분이다.

3. 혁신을 하는 소프트웨어의 적절한 가치 인정

기업의 모든 활동은 돈에 기반한 것이다. 따라서 돈을 빼놓고 소프트웨어의 혁신도 이야기할 수는 없을 것이다. 기존 소프트웨어 산업인 IT서비스도 새로운 시도에는 언제나 돈을 요구했다. IT서비스의 새로운 시도란 새로운 일을 의미했고, 이 일을 한 대가는 수행한 일, 곧 노동의 양을 금전적인 가치로 계산했기 때문이다. 하지만, 소프트웨어의 가치는 노동의 양으로만 평가하는 시대는 지났다. 소프트웨어의 성격이 단순한 업무를 제거하는 것이 목적이기도 하거니와 소프트웨어가 만드는 가치는 코드의 양과 무관하기 때문이다. 그 때문에 소프트웨어도 비즈니스나 문제의 영역에서 문제 해결에 대한 몫을 주장할 수 있는 시대가 도래했다고 할 수 있다. IT서비스에서도 제값 받기 운동이란 꽤 오랜 숙제 이다. 분할 발주로부터 시작해서 최근의 클라우드까지 여러 가지 방법으로 소프트웨어에 대한 제대로된 가치평가를 위한 노력이 지속되어왔다. 그 중 최근 오즈원이라는 스타트업이 하나 등장했는데, 해당 스타트업이 내세운 가치평가 방식이 주목할만하다고 생각한다. 오즈원은 O2O퍼블리셔라는 개념을 쓰고 있는데, 좋은 사업 아이디어를 가진 사업가와 초기 단계 회사를 발굴하여 파트너십을 맺고 공동사업을 진행한다. 이때 오즈원은 IT와 플랫폼 소프트웨어를 제공해 플랫폼을 개발한다. 오프라인에서 역량을 보유했지만 디지털 역량이 부족한 회사에서 파트너십을 맺고 개발을 해주면서, 개발비를 안받는다. 받는 것은 사업에서 나온 매출의 일정부분을 공유 받으며, 실제 사업 운영은 기존 오프라인 업체가 받도록 하고 있다.

{{IMG:4}}
이미지 출처 : 오즈원 "카카오 출신이 O2O 서비스로 만들어드립니다”, 전자신문 2016.06.19

이러한 사업방식은 IT역량이 부족한 기업에 소프트웨어의 가치를 결과론적으로 평가하는 방식을 취한다. 결과적으로 소프트웨어를 전담한 기업은 소프트웨어를 통한 기업의 가치상승에 매진할 테고, 소프트웨어를 개발한 기업은 매출이 올라서 좋은 것이다. 어떤 기업들은 외주만 주면 지속적으로 나혼자 먹을 수 있는 것을 왜 매출을 공유하냐라고 할지 모르겠다. 하지만 소프트웨어의 복잡도가 증가하고, 역할이 중요해지는 시대에는 이러한 시도는 의미가 있다고 할 수 있으며, 매너리즘에 빠진 IT서비스산업에 이러한 사업모델의 등장은 무척 반가운 소식이 아닐 수 없다.

4. 소프트웨어 기업과 사람

- 우리에게는 알파고보다 구글과 하사비스가 필요하다.
This post was contributed to the KT Economic & Management Research Institute on July 6, 2016, under the title "The Importance of Nurturing Software Talent." The contributed content can be viewed below.

[**undefined** www.digieco.co.kr](http://www.digieco.co.kr/KTFront/report/report_issue_trend_view.action?board_seq=10996&board_id=issue_trend&sort_order=&kind=a01&list_page=&list_gubun=&searchtext=&etc1=385&etc2=)

1. Honest Technology Software

Nowadays, with Apple's powerful smartphones threatening Samsung Electronics and Google's AlphaGo defeating Lee Sedol, software seems to be viewed like a gold mine where one only needs to touch a pickaxe to become rich. However, software itself cannot be a gold mine. There's a saying considered one of the golden rules of software: GIGO. Gold in Gold out. Garbage in Garbage out. I believe this value remains unchanged even now, when expectations for software are higher than ever. It's also clear that software is achieving many innovations, but innovative software didn't fall from the sky. Creating software naturally requires people, time, and money, and it happens when there's enough authority for innovation. Regardless of the domain, unacknowledged software always hovers around the periphery, making it difficult to function as an element of innovation. At this point, with the advent of artificial intelligence, the term 'software-centric society' might sound cliché, but for any technology, including AI, it's difficult to expect innovation without it occupying a core position in its respective domain. Unless software is given that much authority and value, no matter how good the technology, it won't create change. This is because software developers are people, and those people can only move when they receive due recognition.

2. The Authority to Fail in Order to Solve Problems

Here's a slide I created recently for a special lecture given to university software majors.

{{IMG:1}}
Software's Changing Position

In the past, the software industry referred to IT service industries and packaged software. Among them, IT services accounted for a very large proportion, and this software played a supporting role, helping with the computerization and efficiency of specific areas. However, recently, software has begun to play a leading role in solving problems, rather than just supporting tasks, and accordingly, the nature of software has changed. The characteristics of this software are that requirements and users are not clear, and software is actively used as a tool for problem-solving. This nature of software makes it difficult to outsource, and the software know-how remains as an asset within the organization. Software companies gain much greater value than physical assets, and the biggest reason software could transform this way was not the emergence of any special technology, but rather the more significant factor of the software's position and role. While it's true that software, as in the traditional IT service industry, is excellent at optimizing processes and saving costs, recent expectations for software go beyond cost reduction, desiring software that directly solves problems, including artificial intelligence. However, for this to happen, it's crucial that such software needs the authority to approach and attempt problems, and the authority to frequently fail and revise work based on those failures. In the case of traditional IT service software, a problem meant financial loss and compensation. Therefore, it could not be considered a tuition fee, and no matter how good an idea was, it could not be applied unless the client opened another wallet. At that time, the best condition for software was to be delivered at a low cost and without errors. Traditional software engineering, which started this way, developed around how to achieve requirements as much as possible.

{{IMG:2}}
Image source: 2014 Information Processing Technology Instructor Preparation Table of Contents http://goo.gl/b7V91p

However, innovation arose from self-directed startups where existing rules did not apply, in areas where such requirements were difficult to discover. This was sometimes even disruptive. While the basic principles of software engineering mentioned earlier are not entirely absent from the latest methodologies, the fact that the nature of a project assumes failure and builds upon it shows a very different aspect in how work is conducted and performance is measured, and it also significantly influences decision-making.

{{IMG:3}}
Latest Software Methodologies

And this culture, in a broad sense, influences the company's culture, software development methods, and even, in a very small way, the code that implements it. Therefore, for large companies to adopt the advantages of startups is not simply about adopting development methodologies, but about embracing the philosophy and culture from which those methodologies emerged. Moreover, the most difficult task is the ideological transformation of all members, including decision-makers, and experiencing improvements by going through cycles is paramount. However, many companies today claim to learn from startups and improve their constitution, but it's questionable whether most are ready to accept such structural changes. How many managers would be willing to watch mistakes happen when the cycle first runs and customers complain? However, if we want to solve difficult problems, we must not be stingy about making mistakes, and we must value the process and system more than the outcome. That can be called a software culture. For this, managers must become smarter and more detailed. It goes without saying that this doesn't mean harassing subordinates in a smart and detailed way. It means constantly contemplating systems and frameworks rather than focusing on finding individual errors of team members. And through this, it's important to naturally change individuals and enable them to control themselves. Control by coercion is fundamentally incompatible with this direction. Just as it's difficult to feel the value of software without experiencing it, it's truly difficult to grasp this corporate culture and method without trying it.

3. Appropriate Recognition of Value for Innovative Software

All corporate activities are based on money. Therefore, we cannot discuss software innovation without money. The existing software industry, IT services, always demanded money for new attempts. A new attempt in IT services meant new work, and the compensation for this work, that is, the amount of labor performed, was calculated in monetary value. However, the era of evaluating software value solely by the amount of labor is over. This is partly because the purpose of software is to eliminate simple tasks, and partly because the value created by software is unrelated to the amount of code. Therefore, it can be said that an era has arrived where software can claim a share in problem-solving in the business or problem domain. Even in IT services, the 'getting paid fairly' movement has been a long-standing challenge. From fragmented orders to recent cloud services, various efforts have been made to properly evaluate software value. Among them, a startup called OzOne recently emerged, and I believe their proposed valuation method is noteworthy. OzOne uses the concept of an O2O publisher, discovering entrepreneurs with good business ideas and early-stage companies, forming partnerships, and jointly conducting business. In this process, OzOne provides IT and platform software to develop the platform. They partner with companies that have offline capabilities but lack digital capabilities, develop for them, and do not charge development fees. Instead, they share a certain portion of the revenue generated from the business, while the actual business operations are handled by the existing offline company.

{{IMG:4}}
Image source: OzOne "Kakao alumni will create O2O services for you," Electronic Times 2016.06.19

This business model takes a results-oriented approach to evaluating the value of software for companies lacking IT capabilities. Consequently, the company dedicated to software will focus on increasing the company's value through software, and the company that developed the software benefits from increased revenue. Some companies might wonder why they should share revenue when they could continuously profit alone by simply outsourcing. However, in an era where software complexity is increasing and its role is becoming more important, such attempts can be said to be meaningful, and the emergence of such business models is very welcome news for the IT service industry, which has fallen into a rut.

4. Software Companies and People

- We need Google and Hassabis more than AlphaGo.

Software is technology, a product, culture, and a service. To be precise, only software can define software, and there is only one thing that connects technology, products, services, and culture: an organization made up of people. It can be said that understanding software has been difficult because we've only tried to think of it within existing frameworks. And because only the technical aspects of software have been emphasized, the understanding of the people and organizations that create software doesn't seem to be very high. Even technologies like artificial intelligence, which are rapidly gaining prominence, have countless developers behind them, and they operate based on the organizational culture and development methodologies of those developers. Many people today seem to have both fear and fantasy regarding AI technology, but AI is also software, and to handle it well, an understanding of the people and organizations that deal with software must also be developed. The key to creating AI comparable to Google's AlphaGo is not the performance of the AI we want to build, but rather learning the culture of Google's software engineers and how they work. That is precisely what we need more than AlphaGo itself.

titleEn: Pokémon GO AR? VR? Why Can't Korea Make It?
contentEn:
Pokémon seems like a truly amazing game. Content that can excite the whole world like this is probably very rare. This isn't the first time Pokémon has become a social issue in Korea. In the early 1990s, Pokémon bread, which included Pokémon stickers, became a social issue in Korea. And now that those children have grown into adults, Pokémon is once again creating social buzz even before its official arrival in Korea. After mentioning Pokémon on Facebook, I received several questions, so I'd like to answer them first.

{{IMG:1}}

1. Is Pokémon an AR game? Is AR rising instead of VR?

**- Strictly speaking, Pokémon is not AR, but MR, a descendant of AR and VR.** Augmented Reality refers to showing additional information in the real world. Strictly speaking, Pokémon Go is not AR but VR. It has a worldview close to a parallel world of the real world. There is only a virtual world that resembles Sokcho, but there is no additional information about Sokcho. However, from a technological perspective, it falls under MR, a descendant of AR.

http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/220743460716
[**Definition and Classification of VR, and 360 Video** VR is quite hot, but it still feels like VR isn't well-defined. The Software Policy Research Institute's V... blog.naver.com](http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/220743460716)

Mixed Reality refers to showing Virtual Reality or Virtual Objects overlaid on the Real World. It's a bit ambiguous to call MR a technology. As I mentioned when explaining AR/MR/VR before, it might be easier to just call it VR. Games are originally meant to be played in a virtual world, not to better understand the real world. Of course, the technology is closer to AR technology because it recognizes surrounding information and objects. And the VR market will not change due to Pokémon Go. It's just that a well-made mobile game has been released. VR hasn't even started yet. The idea that AR is unfolding instead of VR is an overreaction, in my opinion. **- And it's a location-based mobile online game.** In fact, there's one more important thing: it's a location-based mobile online game. While AR provided a new experience, it's not actually the core element of the Pokémon Go game. The core element of the Pokémon Go game is that it's an online game using smartphones based on the user's location. In fact, Pokémon Go can be played with the camera off, using only GPS.

2. So, will mobile AR rise again?

Perhaps because of VR, people keep asking if mobile AR will rise again. The answer to this question is, on the one hand, "no," and on the other hand, "yes."

1) "No." Pokémon Go's success wasn't largely due to AR. Other factors were too strong.

First, the answer "no" is because I believe the core success factor of Pokémon Go was not AR, but rather the influence of the location-based mobile online game, as mentioned earlier. Ultimately, whether a game is well-made or not will be determined not by whether it used AR technology, but by how well the location-based mobile online game was made. Currently, people's reactions are not bad. The success of an online game depends on whether its users create their own culture, and it seems they are already doing so. Therefore, if Pokémon Go is managed properly, its popularity is unlikely to be temporary. Of course, proper management of an online game is not easy, but with a year of know-how from Ingress, I believe they will do well. Some might argue that the novelty of AR attracted many initial users, but I believe the number of initial users is tiny compared to the power of the Pokémon IP. The power of the Pokémon IP is practically a cheat code.

1) However, "Yes." There are already successful AR examples.

However, on the other hand, I can say "yes." There have already been cases where mobile AR technology has shined. Until now, mobile AR technologies have mainly been used briefly in marketing and have not seen real success. Before Pokémon Go, there were several other games, but they failed because taking out the camera was very burdensome. However, there are already apps that have solved this problem: "Snow" and "MSQRD." This technology is AR, or strictly speaking, it's also MR. It uses image recognition technology to create new virtual photos and presents them in a fun, game-like way, while actually performing its primary function as a photo app. Since taking out the camera was burdensome, they approached it as a selfie camera. Furthermore, photo-sharing SNS like Facebook and Instagram increased the desire to use these apps. I can simply say that mobile AR is ultimately about photos. In fact, many Korean users encountering Pokémon Go share AR photos via Facebook. Pokémon Go users' Pokémon locations change as they move, and they try to find suitable locations to share on Facebook. In Pokémon Go, the role of AR is ultimately photography. In the Pokémon Go teaser video, Pokémon trainers appear to be looking at the real space and throwing a ball without looking at their smartphone, but in reality, that's not the case. Trainers end up looking only at the smartphone screen, which becomes similar to the composition of taking a Pokémon photo. And those photos are spread through Facebook and Instagram, gathering people... It's sufficiently serving as a customer acquisition tool. That's as far as I see mobile AR technology going. The hurdles to creating further value are too high.

3. So, will location-based online games succeed?

This isn't the first time for location-based online games either. The weakness of location-based online games is the restriction of time and place. This is far from the convenience of mobile games. For a typical game, I'm somewhat pessimistic about this. Online games require network effects and economies of scale. Could a game with an IP other than Pokémon create such network effects in such a short time? Even Niantic's previous work, which created Pokémon Go, didn't perform exceptionally well in terms of revenue compared to other mobile online games, in my opinion. If a good IP is attached and the game is well-made, the story might change, but an easy entry like Pokémon Go won't be as simple as it seems. The only applicable IP that comes to mind is Minecraft, acquired by MS. However, I believe it has sufficiently demonstrated the effect of small-scale location-based events, rather than global success. Sokcho city really hit the jackpot. Therefore, the desire to create location-based games for regional promotion seems likely to increase. But if you're thinking of making big money, the answer is still no. Unless it's a location-based online "dating" game... Ultimately, it's about targeting a customer base with the ability to pay, and location-based games inherently reduce the customer base, so you need to capture a customer base that can spend a lot of money. Oh, of course, Pokémon, which already has hundreds of millions of users, is an exception.

4. Why can't Korea make Pokémon Go?

1) The difference between Pokémon IP as a video game and an online game

Honestly, I think this question is as foolish as it gets. In the case of Pokémon Go, it was able to grow so large so quickly through the global IP of Pokémon, which is almost unique in the world. Even the US doesn't have something like this. Have you seen Disney make online games? Isn't it strange to ask why we don't have something like this? And the biggest role in creating this global IP was actually played by Nintendo's video games. In contrast, Korea grew centered around online games. Video games, or home console games, are characterized by playing alone for extended periods. Therefore, they often have extensive storylines and worldviews. On the other hand, online games developed in Korea are played by many people sitting in PC bangs. Few people in PC bangs study worldviews. Even with so much StarCraft played, how many Korean users know the StarCraft scenario? It was more urgent to set the speed to maximum and block drone rushes to play one more game. In the Korean game market, which grew centered on such fast-paced, competitive games, it was virtually impossible for stories and worldviews to survive. Even the first online game, "The Kingdom of the Winds," which started with a wonderful story by author Shin Il-sook, ended up having almost nothing to do with the story, didn't it? Therefore, such world-building IPs cannot remain in Korea. So, is the original sin with the Korean game industry? For reference, buying a video game console in Korea was like buying a drug-making machine for a child, and game software was naturally copied in the market. From the beginning, game software survived as online games as a self-preservation measure in such barren land. Ultimately, if we trace the cause, the preference for popular game formats, despite being a gaming powerhouse, prevented the birth of global IPs, and more fundamentally, it was a structure where making other types of games led to failure, with little chance of improvement. Making video game software in Korea is madness. After that, mobile games became popular again. In mobile, which pursues lightness to an even greater degree, even combat is automated, so stories... naturally don't exist. Don't look for a story in Anipang. It's better to read the webtoon if the game is based on one. The game itself was not an environment where it could create its own IP.

2) If we must pinpoint a cause, it's the environment of South Korea, which has weak cultural diversity.

그리고, 포켓몬스터는 전세계 거의 유일무이한 ip다. 아무나 만들고 싶다고 퍽퍽 찍어 만들 수 있는 ip가 아니란 말이다. 그리고 재밌는 것은 포켓몬스터는 지속적으로 재창조되었다. 게임 뿐만 아니라 다양한 형태의 산업에 OSMU로 활용되었고, 일본에는 거대한 2차 저작물 시장인 동인지 시장도 활성화 되있다. 소위 말하는 오덕문화는 이러한 ip가 자라나는데 큰 거름이 된다. 그리고, 이러한 동인지 시장에 금기는 없다. 얼마전 한국에서 시끄러운 "후레자식"은 일본 동인시장에 내놓으면 소프트물이다. 결국 매우 다양하고 거대한 서브컬쳐를 바탕으로 튼튼한 메이저컬쳐가 형성되어있으며, 이러한 문화창작물에 기꺼이 돈을 지불한다. 전세계에서 가장 콘텐츠를 잘 사주는 나라가 일본이다. 그에 반해 한국은 중국하고 앞서거니 뒤서거니...  그러면서 위해하니, 마약이니 온갖 난리는 다 친다. 사주고나 욕 얻어먹으면 덜 억울 할텐데.. 그러니 결국 핑계같지만, 돈되는 성인물이나, 사행성에만 오히려 손을 대는 것 같다. 오버워치를 못만드는 이유가 한국의 게임에 대한 인식 때문이라더니, 한다는 소리가 규제완화로 결제한도 완화를 주장하는 판국을 보면 가슴이 답답하다. 오버워치같은 새로운 경험을 제공하는 잘만든 게임을 만들려면 망할지도 모르는 신선한 게임들에 대한 투자들이 지속적으로 이루어져야 한다. 이로서 기업의 논리보다는 창작자들의 창작욕구를 지속적으로 강화하고 다양한 경험과 실험을 통해 문화적 다양성을 확보해야 한다.  앞서서 내가 위치기반 AR온라인 게임은 기존에도 있었고, 망할 가능성이 높다라고 꼰대같은 소리만 해뎄지만, "난 더 재밌게 만들 수 있어요." 라는 창작자가 있다면 기회를 줘야 한다. 그것이 문화적 다양성이다. 포켓몬go의 주목을 보면서 우리도 저런 기술있는데 부러워하기 이전에.. 기술의 문제가 아니다. SKT에서 정부과제로 게임만든다는 이야기를 듣고... 한숨이 나왔다. SKT가 기술을 안가진게 아니다. 그냥 게임을 만들줄 모를 뿐. 기술이 중한게 아니라 뭘 만들려고 하는지를 고민하는게 낫다.  AR이던 VR이던 게임을 만든다면, 결국 게임성이 가장 중요하고, 영상을 만든다면 영상미와 스토리가 중요하다. 기술이 암만 좋아봐야 콘텐츠의 기본가치가 안된다면, 그냥 기술 demo일 뿐이다.

3) 그리고 냅두면 한국에서는 시들해질거다.

사실 난 한국에서 이 이슈가 그리 오래 가지 않을거라고 본다. 지금은 그저 글로벌 이슈와 속초라는 지역적 제한으로 인해 희귀성으로 인해 더 주목 받는것 같다. 여기에 지자체의 힘까지 보태지고, AR포토의  바이럴 효과까지 겹쳐지고, 무엇보다도 하지말라니까 더 하고 싶은 심리가 겹쳐져, 한국에서는 다 해야 할 것처럼 느끼는것 같다. 하지만 이는 지속성이 있는 이슈들이 아니다. 장기적으로는, 한국은 성인이 게임하는걸 그다지 좋게 보지 않는데다가 위치기반 게임하기에는 너무 바쁘다.  키덜드가 주목 받지만, 여전히 마누라 몰래 하는게 게임이고, 국내 키덜트 시장 규모는 초라하다. 포켓몬 키즈 인구는 제한되어있으며, 한국의 아이들은 터닝메카드에 열광한다. 클래시오브클랜과 같은 출퇴근기간에 할 수 있는 게임은 여전히 인기가 있을 것이다. 물론 그렇다고 흔적도 없이 사라진다는건 아니다. 메니아층으로 인해 상위랭킹은 유지할 가능성이 높다.  물론, 여기에 한가지 예외 변수가 있는데, 포켓몬go의 캐릭터나 아이템이 현금거래가 가능해질 때 이다.  그럼 이제 게임이 아니라 리니지처럼 부업이 된다. 그리고 온라인 커뮤니티성이 강화되어 온라인게임으로서의 성격이 강해진다면, 한국에서도 유효하다고 본다. 한국은 아시다시피 자의인지 타의인지 온라인게임 강국이다.  그러나, 한국을 위해 게임의 성격을 바꿀까? 차라리 닌텐도에서 만들 모바일 포켓몬이라면 모르지만, 외향성이 강한 서양출신인 나인엔틱은 게임 성격을 바꿀 것 같지는 않다.

5. go, go  결국 디지털 콘텐츠의 문화적 다양성 확대가 답이다.

자. 그래서 한국은 뭘해야 하냐고? 알파고의 하사비스가 어릴때 뭘했는지 기억하나? 롤러코스터 게임개발했다. 포켓몬go는 뭐라고? 게임이다. 그리고 게임은 문화콘텐츠다. 문화의 가장 중요한점은 그리고 다양성이다. 지금 당장 돈 벌어들이는게 아니고, 돼지처럼 잘 먹기 위한게 아니라 웃고 울고 그리고 우리가 사는 사회와 주변사람을 돌아보게 하기 위한 것이 콘텐츠다. 콘텐츠산업에서 콘텐츠를 떼버리고 산업만 남겨서는 안된다. 언제까지 우리는 애니메이션에서는 작화만 할 것인가.. 스마트폰에서는 하드웨어만 생산할것인가.. 와 같다.  중요한 것은 소프트웨어고, 보이지 않는 문화 경쟁력이다. 이는 돈으로만 측정되는게 아니다.​​ ​​

Also, Pokémon is an almost unique IP in the world. It's not an IP that anyone can just churn out if they feel like it. And what's interesting is that Pokémon has been continuously re-created. It has been utilized as OSMU (One Source Multi-Use) in various industries beyond just games, and Japan has a massive secondary creation market, the doujinshi market, which is very active. The so-called 'otaku culture' serves as a great fertilizer for such IPs to grow. And there are no taboos in this doujinshi market. The "Bastard" (Hurejasik) that caused a stir in Korea recently would be considered 'soft' material if released in the Japanese doujin market. Ultimately, a robust major culture is formed based on a very diverse and massive subculture, and people willingly pay for these cultural creations. Japan is the country that buys content the most in the world. In contrast, Korea is neck and neck with China... Meanwhile, they cause all sorts of fuss, calling things harmful or like drugs. It would be less unfair if they bought it first and then complained... So, it seems like an excuse, but they only seem to touch profitable adult content or gambling. They say the reason Korea can't make games like Overwatch is due to the perception of games in Korea, but then to hear them advocating for easing payment limits through deregulation makes my chest tight. To create well-made games that offer new experiences like Overwatch, continuous investment in fresh games that might fail is necessary. This way, instead of corporate logic, the creative desires of creators should be continuously strengthened, and cultural diversity should be secured through various experiences and experiments. Earlier, I made 'old-timer' remarks that location-based AR online games already existed and had a high chance of failing, but if there's a creator who says, "I can make it more fun," they should be given a chance. That is cultural diversity. Looking at the attention Pokémon Go is getting, before envying them for having such technology... it's not a matter of technology. Hearing that SKT is making a game as a government project... I sighed. It's not that SKT doesn't have the technology. They just don't know how to make games. It's not technology that's important, but rather contemplating what you want to create. Whether it's AR or VR, if you're making a game, gameplay is ultimately the most important; if you're making a video, visual aesthetics and story are important. No matter how good the technology is, if it doesn't contribute to the fundamental value of the content, it's just a tech demo.

3) And if left alone, it will fade in Korea.

Honestly, I don't think this issue will last very long in Korea. Currently, it seems to be gaining more attention due to its rarity, stemming from it being a global issue and the regional restriction to Sokcho. Added to this are the efforts of local governments, the viral effect of AR photos, and above all, the psychological tendency to want to do something more when told not to, making it feel like everyone in Korea has to do it. But these are not sustainable issues. In the long term, Korea doesn't view adults playing games very favorably, and people are too busy for location-based games. While 'kidults' are gaining attention, gaming is still often done secretly from one's spouse, and the domestic kidult market size is meager. The Pokémon kids' population is limited, and Korean children are enthusiastic about Turning Mecard. Games that can be played during commutes, like Clash of Clans, will still be popular. Of course, that doesn't mean it will disappear without a trace. It's highly likely to maintain a high ranking due to its dedicated fanbase. However, there's one exceptional variable here: when Pokémon Go characters or items become tradable for cash. Then it becomes a side job, like Lineage, rather than just a game. And if its online community aspect is strengthened, making it more like an online game, then I believe it would be effective in Korea too. As you know, Korea is a powerhouse in online games, whether by choice or by circumstance. But would they change the game's nature for Korea? Perhaps if it were a mobile Pokémon game made by Nintendo, but Niantic, being a Western company with a strong outward focus, is unlikely to change the game's nature.

5. Go, Go: Ultimately, expanding cultural diversity in digital content is the answer.

So, what should Korea do? Do you remember what Demis Hassabis of AlphaGo did when he was young? He developed roller coaster games. What is Pokémon Go? It's a game. And games are cultural content. And the most important aspect of culture is diversity. Content isn't about making money right now, or eating well like a pig; it's about making us laugh and cry, and reflecting on the society we live in and the people around us. We shouldn't remove 'content' from the 'content industry' and leave only 'industry'. It's like asking, "How long will we only do animation drawings in animation... or only produce hardware for smartphones?" What's important is software, and invisible cultural competitiveness. This isn't measured solely by money.

It's reported that Pokémon Go, the recently released location-based AR game, is even boosting Nintendo's stock price.

[**Nintendo Stock Soars 25% on Pokémon Go Popularity…Market Cap Increases by 8 Trillion Won** (SEOUL=Yonhap News) Reporter Moon Jeong-sik= Shares of Japanese game maker Nintendo surged like a spring following the release of its new mobile game, Pokémon Go. www.yonhapnews.co.kr](http://www.yonhapnews.co.kr/bulletin/2016/07/11/0200000000AKR20160711135000009.HTML)

While AR is touted as a new technology, games with this concept were actually proposed a very long time ago. Below is an idea I proposed in 2009, which is almost identical to Pokémon Go, except for the running aspect.

http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/70084903863
                                [**[Idea] Multiplayer Game Using Augmented Reality in Physical Space** Title: Multiplayer Game Using Augmented Reality in Physical Space First Draft Date: October 12, 2009 0. Concept... blog.naver.com](http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/70084903863)

I'm not saying I'm brilliant. In fact, a similar type of game was proposed back in 2007.

What exactly made these games different from Pokémon Go? I think there's only one difference: brand. Two brands are hidden behind this success: Google and Pokémon. Pokémon already has high brand recognition, to the extent that Pokémon bread was a social issue in the past. Since it's already familiar through animation, no separate marketing costs are incurred for scenario or character learning. Furthermore, the scenario that stimulates nurturing and collecting desires is a perfect fit for this type of game. Moreover, Google's Pokémon-related Easter egg was revealed in 2014, and it even became a topic for April Fool's Day.

And Niantic Labs, which created Pokémon Go, is a company that originated from Google.

**Google Spins Off Niantic Labs, Specializing in Augmented Reality Game Development** Just two days after announcing its organizational restructuring, Google announced the separation of its augmented reality unit, Niantic Labs, into an independent company. This means Niantic Labs will not be included in the new parent company, Alphabet. Alphabet is scheduled to officially launch at the end of this year and will consist of Google and other business units. A Google spokesperson stated that the spin-off would accelerate Niantic's growth and allow it to work more closely with investors and partners in the entertainment sector. www.itworld.co.kr

http://www.itworld.co.kr/news/95003

Therefore, the success of Pokémon Go can be seen not as a coincidence, but as an achievement brought about by the convergence of strong brands. Some people in Korea might wonder why we can't create a game like Pokémon Go. Before that, what I want to tell them is that we never created Pokémon. That's why it's difficult. If we were to make such a game using Pororo, which targets toddlers, it would 100% fail. Recently, someone who filed a lawsuit against 'Hurejasik' mentioned 'Pororo' and 'Dooly,' and in Korea, where games and comics are often considered solely for children, I believe it's still too early for such a foundation to be built. While I hope for the global success of Korean cultural content, I think this is an opportunity to reflect on whether our perception is still stuck in arcades and comic book stores for delinquent teenagers.

Let's also cultivate world-class IPs.

ps. I think Pokémon Go's AR success is like Avatar for 3D TV. It's highly likely to be the beginning and end of smartphone-based AR games. Drawing a parallel from past experience, the Tamagotchi craze didn't spawn successful successors. Among the same genre after Pokémon, only Digimon was a successful model, but it couldn't surpass Pokémon. And crucially, gamers don't like moving around. They don't have that much free time either. Ultimately, it raises a question mark regarding its sustainability.

I hope this post will be the last one about the "Bastard" lawsuit. Through this incident, I learned about the public's perception of webtoons, and conversely, how ignorant our society is about children's culture. If we don't understand, we can't diagnose or help them.

{{IMG:1}}

South Park

1. What is a Webtoon?

First, I realized that many people, including the webtoon plaintiff, are ignorant about webtoons. While 8 million webtoon users are mentioned, the majority of them are in their 20s and 30s. And many of them consume webtoons lightly, like slice-of-life comics shared on social media. They might be called webtoon consumers, but they don't know everything about webtoons, nor are they what you'd call "hardcore fans." For them, webtoons might be nothing more than billboards.

1) Webtoons are Cultural Content

To be considered a demographic that properly understands webtoons, one should at least have webtoons they regularly follow every week. One of the biggest differences between webtoons and print comics is their serialized nature. They are closer to dramas than movies. While webtoons are an extension of comics, their production costs are lower and their reliance on the artist is higher compared to traditional comic books. This allows for an incomparably diverse range of subjects and themes compared to other media that are highly dependent on capital. This is precisely why the broadcasting and film industries, which demand only verified content, are paying close attention to webtoons. Their dilemma is that while broadcasting and film require significant capital investment, they must minimize risk, which often runs counter to the novelty of subject matter and themes. To bridge this gap, they began to look at webtoons. It's no coincidence that many popular dramas and films recently are based on webtoons. The plaintiff, in their complaint, mentioned Pororo and Dooly as examples of proper comics, but they clearly haven't seen the original work by Kim Soo-jung. The episode depicting the Iraq War is one of the most memorable works of my life. Dooly's origin itself was changed to an animal because the author was afraid of being arrested for drawing social commentary... **-- Episode 95, March 1991, Gulf War II --** 『Dooly』 is by no means unrelated to current events, and this episode, in particular, seems to be remembered as shocking by many readers. Dooly's gang divides into teams, shaking hands with Iraqi soldiers and multinational coalition soldiers, confronting each other. Up to the middle, it proceeds in a comedic tone, with Iraqi and American soldiers even reconciling. However, on the 10th page, the atmosphere dramatically shifts as the two soldiers step on landmines and are blown up. Afterward, scenes of devastation follow: a destroyed city, a girl left alone after her parents died, and people eating a dead sheep because there's nothing else to eat. After Dooly's gang gives up collecting bombs and leaves, it's revealed that the girl's older brother was the Iraqi soldier who was blown up by a landmine right in front of her, intensifying the tragedy, and the episode ends there. Overall, the anti-war message is clear.

[*The Patriot missile, which was a hot topic during the Gulf War, also appears in the work.*](http://egloos.zum.com/shaw/v/3693971)[*http://egloos.zum.com/shaw/v/3693971*](http://egloos.zum.com/shaw/v/3693971)

Here, we will present the order of each episode of 『Dooly』, primarily based on the original magazine publication, and briefly add special notes. The serialized version does not specifically include the title of each episode. egloos.zum.com

http://egloos.zum.com/shaw/viewer/3693971

The problem is severe from the very idea of webtoons being only for the Pororo age group. You should be using Juniver, you've chosen the wrong service. The role of webtoons lies in their diversity, breathing with the public. While there are charts that mock the predictable stories of Korean morning dramas, such charts cannot be created for webtoons. It's safe to say that most predictable stories are cut, and there are almost no webtoons where you can predict the conclusion from the beginning. The plaintiff's "Bastard" is no exception. It's difficult to judge a work based on just a few expressions.

2) Regulation of Webtoon Copyrights

Since webtoons are free content based on an internet advertising model, some people seem to think they are public performances that anyone can view and use. Webtoons are clearly the author's copyrighted work. Furthermore, the right to choose that work belongs to the reader. It is the platform's competitiveness to present this work to the appropriate audience. However, only works defined as 19+ under the Youth Protection Act require age verification. The scope where subjectivity cannot intervene in the 19+ debate is limited to direct expressions. Things like actual stabbing scenes, or nudity beyond a woman's toplessness. "Bastard" avoids all such expressions. However, the scope of sexual imagination or violent expression is actually more attributable to direction and story than to such direct scenes. Therefore, it is usually controlled at an appropriate level by censorship bodies, and often regulated more broadly than the law. And, in the case of webtoons, due to the nature of comics, they also have the effect of being viewed with less repulsion. Expressiveness weakens from live-action to drawings, and from drawings to text only. Therefore, it is natural to see webtoons having a broader range of expression than live-action, or video content. However, on the other hand, imagination has the effect of filling that void more strongly than live-action, so rather than cutting it with a knife, it is right for those with professional knowledge or within the relevant cultural industry to appropriately self-regulate.

3) Webtoons are Cultural Content

Amidst all this, the controversy over central pre-censorship of a thriller webtoon ("Bastard") is a critical issue that could infringe on creative freedom and lead to a contraction of the entire Korean cultural industry. The plaintiff probably didn't understand this well, but it's close to a challenge to the cultural sector that has worked for decades to establish self-regulation. In fact, I was surprised that many people didn't even understand the meaning of self-regulation. Self-regulation doesn't mean central regulation has disappeared. The plaintiff should have filed a complaint with the central regulatory body, not a lawsuit. This negates the current self-regulatory system and advocates a return to the past dictatorial era.

2. Do Violent Webtoons Really Make Children Violent?

The most common argument I heard when discussing the "Bastard" lawsuit was that "violent scenes" are harmful to children. And the conclusion is that they can make children violent. I agree with some of it, but I disagree with some (actually most) of it.

1) Where Does Children's Violence Come From?

Let's talk a bit about violence. Will children, clean as paper, not use violence? We could go into the debate of human nature being good or evil, but any parent who has raised a child knows the answer: "No." Children are inherently purely violent. To be precise, it's more accurate to say they are instinctive. They generally lack proper control over the intensity of violence. This is because they haven't learned about pain or developed empathy for others. However, a repulsion to blood does exist. This doesn't seem to be learned. It's probably closer to a fundamental instinct to protect oneself from threats to safety during a long evolutionary process. People who lack or have a weak version of this (it's difficult to call it a disease) can be called psychopaths. In fact, there's a scene where the protagonist of "Bastard" recalls childhood memories, and this could be that part. (In the webtoon, he sealed away that memory himself. And it's one of the biggest twists in the theme.) This is likely one of the biggest factors that puts a brake on children's violence. And I agree with the psychiatrist who, in a previous post, referred to "children from normal families" as those who have gone through a less externally stimulated upbringing, suggesting this effect would be significant for them. Furthermore, sensitivity to violence isn't limited to children. Adults also exist who are sensitive to horror, disaster, and thriller genres. Honestly, I myself have vivid memories of the gunshot wounds in Robocop 1, which I saw as a child, and it scared me for a long time. Since this can be traumatic, I also recommend that children use media and computers under parental supervision. This cannot be definitively stated as it varies depending on the child's condition. But can only a sensory aversion to violence truly prevent violence? I don't think so. Violence isn't just physical; it also exists in social or indirect forms, and there are many webtoons that use this as their subject matter.

2) Does Insensitivity to Violence Reinforce Violence?

Moreover, sensitivity to violence weakens through various stimuli as one grows up. I admit that this has the effect of making one insensitive to violence. The professions most insensitive to blood are soldiers, firefighters, police officers, and doctors. They continuously see blood, suppressing this instinct, and learn that it is unrelated to their own safety. This is unrelated to the reinforcement of their own violence. Children feel scared when they see an injection, but they become okay with it as they grow older. When they are children, getting hit by their mom feels so scary, but when they go to the military and get hit with a bat, they might just say, "Oh, shit." This is the result of such learning. In conclusion, this growth is very normal, and insensitivity to violence is unavoidable as one grows up. Ultimately, the degree of sensitivity to violence is not a direct control mechanism for committing violence.

3) Suppressing Violence During Growth is Understanding the Absurdity of Violence

그러면 폭력의 기재를 억누를 수 있는 가장 큰 원인은 무엇일까? 바로 공감과 사회성이다. 피해자로서 느끼는 1차적인 아픔이 아니라, 바로 폭력의 부조리함에 대한 학습이다. 폭력으로 인한 것이 어떠한 영향을 미치는지를 사회적으로 아는 것이다. 이것에 대한 학습이전에 법으로 막아두고는 있지만, 법으로만 폭력이 나쁘다는 것을 아는 것은 앞서말한 싸이코패스와 가깝다고 할 수 있다. 이 분들이 기준이 될수는 없으니 그냥 보통 사람들 이야기를 해보자. 때문에 방송통신윤리 위원회의 공감능력이 존재하는 보통사람을 위한 폭력에 대한 규제는 “폭력을 찬양”하는지에 대해 중점을 두고 있다. “폭력에 대한 표현”이 아니다. 후레자식은 단연코 폭력을 찬양하지 않는다. 오히려 앞서말한 폭력의 부조리함을 이해하는데 도움이 된다.

4) 웹툰 미디어의 10대와 대중 공감의 우수성

앞서 말한 웹툰의 특성은 10대에게 폭력의 부조리함을 이해시키는데 효과적인 미디어다. 제작 비용이 싸서 진입장벽이 낮으며, 심지어는 직접 생산이 가능한 구조는 젊은 창작자들에게 높은 자유도와 낮은 진입장벽을 선사했다. 결과적으로 매우 어린작가들의 등단이 가능한 구조며(실제 고등학생 작가도 있다.) 10대에 대한 이해도가 높다. 그들이 말하는 것, 행동하는 것을 이해한다. 또한 다양한 사상과 생각, 상상력을 버무리고, 경쟁을 통해 문학적, 대중적 요소가 높은 것들이 상위로 올라오는 구조이다. 때문에 폭력에 대한 굉장히 실증적이고 다양한 해석들을 해준다. 난 오히려 사전검열을 강하게 거치는 깨끗한 방송에서 정말 십대들을 위한 솔직한 이야기를 한 적이 있는가? 라고 묻고 싶다. 학생사회의 1진에 대해 성인들은 얼마나 알고 있는가? 그저 학교폭력을 당하면 신고해라. 가 다 이지 않나? 선생님들의 교권이나 땅에 떨어진 상황이나 아이들의 학업에 대한 고민, 그리고 그들의 꿈에 대해 어떤 미디어가 이야기를 해주고 있나. 웹툰에서 1진물의 위해성은 여전히 논란의 거리이긴 하다. 웹툰에서 상상하는 멋진 1진은 사실 “나라면 다르겠지”라고 느끼는 피해자들이 그린 상상속의 1진의 모습이기 떄문이기도 하다. 그러나, 이러한 상상력은 성인들의 내가 재벌총수가 되면.. 과 다를바가 없다. 성장기 아이들 사회에서 폭력도 하나의 계급이기 때문이고, 이를 완전히 제거하기는 어려울것이다. 그렇다면 이 아이들에게 필요한 것은 앞서 말한 폭력의 사회적 부조리함을 더욱 가르쳐야 한다. 적어도 웹툰의 1진물들은 “폭력 찬양”은 19금에 걸리기 때문에, 작가의 실력에 따라 차이는 나지만, 폭력을 찬양하는 작품은 없다. 오히려 성인이 된 1진이 학창시절에 무심코 했던 폭력이 어떤 끔찍한 결과를 가져오는지에 대한 소재도 정면으로 그린 작품들도 존재한다. 간단히 말해 방송에서 외면한 학교 폭력에 대한 진짜 심각한 논의는 웹툰에서 다루어지고 있고, 어른들의 미디어에서는 아이들을 어떻게 벌줄지와 격리할지만 고민하고 있다. 어쩌면 당연한지도 모르겠다. 생산,소비자가 모두 10대가 아니니.. 요즘에는 그 범위를 넓혀 최근에는 가족간의 폭력까지 소재의 범위를 넓혔다. 그런 웹툰을 보고 펑펑 울었다는 댓글이 달리는 요즘이다. 과연 우리의 미디어가 가야할 길이 어디일까? 이런 웹툰을 다시 중앙 규제로 회귀하자는 말인가?

3. 사회를 비추고 사회를 치유하는 웹툰

그제 영화 곡성을 보았다. 이 영화도 15금이 아닌 부모의 지도하라면 15세 이하도 시청가능한 15가다. 솔직히 말해 후레자식보다 훨씬 잔인했고, 후레자식보다 혼란스럽게 떡밥을 늘어놓았다. 이 영화도 19금 논란이 좀 있는 듯하지만, 그럼에도 불구하고 엄청난 인기를 끌고 있으며 이러한 문제가 수면 위로 올라오고 있지 않다. 이는 꽤 수준 높은 작품이기 때문일 것이고, 영화를 보는 사람들은 중간에 그만둘 수 없기 때문일 것이다. 후레자식처럼 고소자처럼 몇편만보고 이거 19금걸어야 되. 이러지는 않는다는것이다. 잔인한 표현이 많았지만, 끝나고 나면 피에 대한 기억보다는 스토리와 떡밥만 떠올랐다. 이것이 연출과 스토리의 힘일것이다. 사실, 몇개의 웹툰이 떠오르는 스토리를 가지고 있었는데, 고비용의 영화에서 저정도의 감독의 자유로운 이야기가 펼쳐졌다는 점은 그만큼 우리의 문화계가 성숙한 증거일것 같다. 오늘날의 웹툰은 사회를 비추고, 사회를 치유하고 문화를 풍요롭게 한다. 어릴적 불량만화방에 대한 기억만 있는 분들이 웹툰에 대해 심각한 오해가 있는듯하다. 일본의 Anime나 망가와 달리 한국의 웹툰은 사회적으로 성장해가고 있다. 일본의 영화계가 한국의 영화계를 부러워하는 일이 만화에서도 일어나고 있다. 물론 모든 웹툰이 좋다는건 아니다. 포털의 연재물이 아닌 자유기고가 가능한 커뮤니티의 웹툰들은 아이들의 욕망만을 여과없이 뱉어내는경우도 존재한다. 하지만, 이러한 위험을 스스로 걸러내지 못할만큼 우리의 문화계와 사용자들과 독자들이 무식쟁이들은 아니라고 본다. 이를 역행하지는 말자.

titleEn: [Son of a Bitch Lawsuit] The Youth Protection Act is not a Child Protection Act.
contentEn:
1. Child protection cannot be a reason in the 'Bastard' controversy.

It seems many people are most confused about this in the 'Bastard' controversy, but the Juvenile Protection Act aims to protect adolescents, not children. Children must fundamentally be subjects assumed to be under parental supervision. Even in the case of daycare centers, it's assumed they are always under the supervision of teachers. Parents who simply hand a computer or smartphone to a child and then tell them not to watch 'Bastard' are actually infringing upon the rights of adolescents. I hope this point is not confused. Intermediate age ratings like 12 and 15 are recommendations, not 12-rated or 15-rated restrictions. For children, this means parents should manage their viewing based on these recommendations. Even if we concede a hundred times that Naver has a problem, it would only be for not indicating the recommended age. (However, this webtoon is not popular with children anyway, and children would show strong aversion to it. Children do not like strong stimuli. Don't mistakenly think children will like it. Forcing them to watch it would be child abuse.) If all content rated 'G' (General Audience) had to protect children, then all of it would need 12-rated or 15-rated restrictions. Especially news and social affairs sections. Then, ultimately, the worst situation in the world would occur, where all internet content would require real-name verification, something even communist parties don't do for all content. (It seems there are people who want that. You're not from Namsan, are you?)

2. Youth protection should not infringe upon the freedom of artistic consumption.

The Juvenile Protection Act should also be approached from the perspective of laws concerning the exploitation of adolescents. That's why the Cinderella Law, having nothing else to attach, ended up with something strange like 'the right to sleep'. If the Cinderella Law's intent is to be followed, then late-night self-study should also be abolished. While some argue for blocking various things due to adolescents' immature values, explicit sexual content or violent content should indeed be blocked. (In fact, gore, which is violent content, is not preferred by adults in Korea either. It can be considered almost non-existent here.) I agree with blocking content depicting sexual fantasies because adolescents are in the midst of secondary sexual characteristics. However, I believe it is better to grant adolescents the right to view serious, especially good, content that deals with other social issues, even if it might be somewhat uncomfortable. This is because it infringes upon adolescents' freedom of artistic consumption, rather than protecting them.

3. Distinguish the controversy and separate the frames. Understand why people are angry and calling others 'kkondae'. Children vs. Adolescents, Pornography vs. Cultural Content.

This controversy is structured as a 2x2 matrix. One axis is **Children and Adolescents**, and the other is **Pornography and Cultural Content**. This is because content like 'Bastard' is not gore or pornography. And the reason many creators and fans are angry and calling others 'kkondae' is precisely because their beloved cultural content was treated in the same way as gore and pornography. In comics, this kind of controversy is, in fact, nothing new.

titleEn: Future Education Methods to Break Free from Being an Old-Fashioned Boss
contentEn:
My blog is quite noisy today because of yesterday's "Bastard" post.

http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/220752944378
[**I'm more worried about parents who don't understand "Bastard."** I saw a post on my timeline expressing concern about children watching the webtoon "Bastard," which is rated for all ages. ... blog.naver.com](http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/220752944378)

Since I've started, let's finish it. I've criticized, so shouldn't I offer an alternative? The reason I criticized them as "꼰대" (old-fashioned, preachy elders) is that they tried to interfere with creative and free thinking by imposing their didactic educational methods on the public. Fundamentally, their way of thinking and mine are different. Many people might think I'm just laughing and chatting with kids without much thought, so I'd like to share my perspective. Last year, I looked at a lot of materials related to software education, and as I delved into future education, my thoughts began to solidify. I'm not giving lectures or anything, but I'd like to share this story.

1. The Crisis of Education Focused on Korean, English, and Math

Alvin Toffler, who recently passed away, warned about Korean education, but to make it easier to understand, let me first show you a picture.

{{IMG:1}}

Future Education Framework P21, Source: http://www.p21.org/

In the center, you see "3R," right? Reading, Writing, Arithmetic. In Korean, that simply translates to "Korean, English, Math." It's not that their importance has diminished. However, the time is coming when those alone will no longer be enough. First, the "4C" above: Critical Thinking can be seen as problem-solving ability. The remaining Communication, Collaboration, and Creativity are all emphasized in recent education, and on the right, there are Information Media and Technology skills. All of this speaks to pro-digital, not anti-digital. Recently, someone at PitchOne Media, who advocates the pseudo-scientific "game brain theory," talked about Apple and anti-digital ideas. If you teach that way, you won't even get close to Apple. If someone talks about digital affecting the frontal lobe, just assume they're a charlatan trying to sell books.

**"If you want to raise an Apple employee, don't buy them a smartphone until they enter university; the moment you do, your child's life is worth 5 won." A chilling warning.** "Save your children from smartphones." Smartphones are now carried by almost all elementary school children, and it's almost commonplace to see preschoolers staring intently at videos in restaurants. Even elementary school students feel they can't go without one because their peers have them. Once they get one, they become addicted to smartphones and mobile games, neglecting studies and even exercise. For parents struggling with smartphone addiction, a guide-like video has emerged... www.pitchone.co.kr

http://www.pitchone.co.kr/?p=5940

On the left, "Life and Career Management"... In Korea, parents often do this for their children, which is a serious situation ㅜㅜ This is listed as a necessary skill for students. Parents shouldn't do it for them. Performance evaluation is about assessing the process, but parents who say they have too much to do and no time for Korean, English, and Math are essentially saying they'll only focus on the green part. Please, I urge you to feel a sense of crisis. "But college admissions will be fine," you might think... A shocking fact I heard recently from PD Jung Chan-pil of the Future Classroom Network's Flipped Classroom at an Edutech Forum:

Gangnam cram schools are hiding the fact that universities are starting to abandon specialized high schools. Students admitted from them are often weak, unable to do things properly, and not preferred by companies, leading to poor employment rates. The data already shows this.

I was skeptical too. But then, the news broke...

http://news.naver.com/main/read.nhn?mode=LSD&mid=sec&oid=421&aid=0002141653&sid1=001
[**Number of 'specialized high school' students decreases, 'autonomous high school' students increases among new Seoul university students** Jongro Haneul Education, analysis of University Alimi results... Korea University has the most graduates from specialized/autonomous private high schools (Seoul=News1) Reporter Kwon Hyung-jin. Among new students at major Seoul universities this year, the number of students from specialized high schools and ... news.naver.com](http://news.naver.com/main/read.nhn?mode=LSD&mid=sec&oid=421&aid=0002141653&sid1=001)

Autonomous high schools (자율고) are different from autonomous private high schools (자사고). These are autonomous public high schools (자율공립고등학교). Of course, this might be a temporary trend. Among specialized high schools, science high schools, from what I recall, had decent evaluations for problem-solving skills and such, so they might be different from foreign language high schools... Anyway, the indicators show this. Educational policies like innovative elementary schools, free semester system in middle schools, and autonomous and specialized high schools are being implemented based on the framework of future education.

2. So, why talk about webtoons?

Webtoons are a representative cultural content for teenagers. They fall under the digital media mentioned earlier, and creativity can be gained through diverse information and various works. That's why education often talks about combining Art and Tech. And I believe that creative media like webtoons help expand children's thinking. Also, when children grow up and create content like "Reply 1988," webtoons will be there. "Reply 2010" will definitely feature webtoons. Restricting such popular culture stifles creativity. That education framework doesn't include regulation or ethics. Instead, "civic consciousness" is emphasized in education, which means living together with people different from oneself, not advocating dictatorship. The uniformity they advocated actually goes against this.

3. My Educational Philosophy

Since I'm not a teacher, it's a bit much to call it an educational philosophy. Please understand that from here on, my subjective views are heavily mixed in. The education I envision for children is empathy, broadening horizons of thought, imagination, and daring to create. Scores are not important here.

1) Empathy

For empathy, I ask my child why they thought that way. My son, whose vocabulary is still limited, always shouts "I don't know!", but my daughter, now 7, speaks incredibly well. Or, if there's a misunderstanding, I logically persuade the child.

http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/220312177291
[**What I felt while teaching my daughter: The problem of lost responsibility in Korea** 1. My daughter Saebom's story. My 6-year-old daughter often gets scolded these days. For some reason, even after being scolded, she doesn't improve... blog.naver.com](http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/220312177291)

2) Broadening Horizons of Thought

My wife dislikes this part a bit, but I tend to push my children to think differently. In neuroscience, creativity refers to the act of connecting things that are not obvious. Connecting the sea and a boat is easy, but connecting the sea and a skunk requires creativity, and it's said that activation of distant brain regions actually occurs, leading to creativity. That's why I often tell my kids things that make them confused (my wife dislikes it, saying I teach them strange things). I tell them that a cute rabbit can be scary, a scary bear can be cute, that the dinosaurs we know didn't always fight, and that 1+1=2, which they learned in kindergarten, might not be natural. Recently, I was introduced to and bought a book about dinosaurs that presented different ideas from what we commonly know, and I gave it to them as a gift.

{{IMG:2}}

**Were there dinosaurs that liked flowers?**

Author
Lee Jeong-mo, Noh Jeong-im
Publisher
Charlie Book
Release
2014.09.01.

http://book.naver.com/bookdb/book_detail.php?bid=8019107

Thanks to this, when other children say dinosaurs are extinct, they can say, "No, they're not?" (Haha, but teachers might dislike it.) As mentioned earlier, webtoons greatly help broaden horizons of thought, and media depicts various social phenomena with artistic merit. And to know light, one must know darkness. Just as you can't draw light without drawing shadows. I have such an educational philosophy.

3) Imagination and (Making) Challenges

As I mentioned before, I'm very interested in software education. I used to be a software engineer, and I loved drawing and creating things. Perhaps she takes after me, but my daughter also loves to draw. Her drawing skills are improving surprisingly fast, perhaps because she attends an art academy that also functions as a kindergarten, but I'm a little worried that she might become fixated on the aforementioned drawing formulas. However, technology is one of the fastest ways to achieve one's goals and one of the ways to express imagination. In that sense, I encourage her to learn technology, create stories, imagine, and challenge herself.
